scores.reason: Consumer financial field experiment showing a default-style option anchors people just above a floor and moves nominal behavior without moving the real outcome — bears on the preset-multiplier and vanity-metric worries, though it studies autopay shrouding rather than enrolment design itself.

EU consumer setting, self-directed investment choices: shows defaults shift the chosen level with medium-to-large effects and that imposed or refused defaults damage perceived trustworthiness — directly informs both the preset-level decision (C3/C4) and the manipulation-risk concern (C5).

Directly quantifies how much smaller default effects are in steady state once attrition and opt-out are counted — the strongest available evidence for the support team's counter-argument and squarely on C1/C2, employer setting notwithstanding.

Gives a clean 23pp effect size for auto-enrolment and shows the effect shrinks when incentives are low, choices are simple, and opting out is easy — exactly the conditions of a small liquid round-up feature, so it directly informs the entry decision (C1).

The classic evidence that auto-enrolment anchors most participants at the preset rate for years — highly relevant to C3, but it is an old employer-plan study placed in a scored slot when the brief explicitly deprioritizes the foundational pension literature.
A recent review covering auto-enrolment defaults and their engagement downsides satisfies the brief's ask for a synthesis, though it is employer-plan focused and the abstract reports no effect sizes.

Answers the brief's persistence question head-on: participation and contribution gains at 12 months attenuate sharply by 36 months, with distributional detail (inequality falls) — central to C2 and C5 despite the retirement-plan setting.

Closest structural analog to the product — liquid, anytime-withdrawable savings — showing pure opt-in yields ~0.7% take-up but excellent 12-month persistence among choosers; directly informs the entry decision and the enrolment-vs-engagement trade-off (C1/C2).

Foundational slot: a well-known demonstration that a consumer fintech nudge helped most users while harming an overdraft-prone subgroup — real background for the brief's distributional concern (C5), though not the one canonical paper on savings defaults.

Foundational slot: the originating paper on active and enhanced active choice as an enrolment design — the exact third option in Decision 1; a newcomer weighing active choice against opt-out would misread the list without it.
